source_text: Hoc unitatis sacramentum, hoc uinculum concordiae inseparabiliter cohaerentis ostenditur, quando in euangelio tunica Domini Iesu Christi non diuiditur omnino nec scinditur, sed sortientibus de ueste Christi, quis Christum potius indueret, integra uestis accipitur et incorrupta adque indiuidua tunica possidetur. loquitur ac dicit scriptura diuina: de tunica autem, quia de superiore parte non consutilis sed per totum textilis fuerat, dixerunt ad inuicem: non scindamus llam sed sortiamur de ea, cuius sit. unitatem ille portabat de superiore parte uenientem id est de caelo et a patre uenientem quae ab accipiente ac possidente scindi omnino non poterat, sed totam semel et solidam firmitatem inseparabiliter obtinebat. possidere non potest indumentum Christi qui scindit et diuidit ecclesiam Christi. contra denique cum Salomone moriente regnum eius et populus scinderetur, Achias propheta Hieroboam regi obuius factus in campo in duodecim scissuras uestimentum suum discidit dicens: sume tibi decem scissuras, quia haec dicit Dominus: ecce scindo regnum de manu Salomonis et dabo tibi decem sceptra, et duo sceptra erunt ei propter seruum meum Dauid et propter Hierusalem ciuitatem quam elegi, ut ponam nomen meum illic. cum duodecim tribus Israel scinderentur, uestimentum suum propheta Achias discidit. at uero quia Christi populus non potest scindi, tunica eius per totum textilis et cohaerens diuisa a possidentibus non est: indiuidua, copulata, conexa ostendit populi nostri qui Christum induimus concordiam cohaerentem. sacramento uestis et signo declarauit ecclesiae unitatem.
thought_title: The seamless tunic as sign of the Church's indivisible unity
orientation: Cyprian is explaining how the seamless tunic of Christ in the Gospel, and Ahijah's torn garment in the Old Testament, both signify the unity of the Church.
pass_a_gloss: This sacred sign of unity, this bond of harmony inseparably cohering, is shown when in the gospel the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ is not divided at all nor torn, but when they cast lots for the clothing of Christ, to see who would rather put on Christ, the whole garment is received and the uncorrupted and undivided tunic is possessed. The divine Scripture speaks and says: but about the tunic, because it was not sewn from the upper part but woven throughout, they said to one another: let us not tear it but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be. That man was carrying the unity coming from the upper part, that is, coming from heaven and from the Father, which could not be torn at all by the one receiving and possessing it, but was obtaining the whole, once and solid, firmness inseparably. He cannot possess the garment of Christ who tears and divides the Church of Christ. On the contrary, finally, when at Solomon's death his kingdom and people were being divided, the prophet Ahijah, having met King Jeroboam in the field, tore his garment into twelve pieces, saying: take for yourself ten pieces, because the Lord says this: behold, I am tearing the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and I will give you ten scepters, and two scepters will be for him because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem the city which I chose, to place my name there. When the twelve tribes of Israel were being divided, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But truly, because the people of Christ cannot be divided, his tunic, woven throughout and cohering, was not divided by those possessing it: undivided, joined, connected, it shows the cohering harmony of our people who have put on Christ. By the sacred sign of the garment and by the sign he declared the unity of the Church.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'sacred sign' for sacramentum, not 'sacrament'.
The glossary requires 'harmony' for concordia, not 'concord'.
The glossary requires 'tunic' for tunica, not 'garment' or 'robe'.
The glossary requires 'Church' for ecclesia, not 'assembly' or 'congregation'.
Indumentum is a general term for clothing, distinct from tunica; 'garment' preserves the distinction.

pass_b_english: This sacred sign of unity, this bond of harmony holding inseparably together, is shown in the Gospel when the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ is not divided or torn at all. Instead, as they cast lots for Christ's clothing to see who would rather put on Christ, the garment is received whole, and the tunic is possessed undamaged and undivided. Divine Scripture speaks and says: "Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top, so they said to one another, 'Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it will be'" (John 19:23-24). He bore the unity that comes from above—that is, from heaven and from the Father—which could not be torn at all by the one who received and possessed it, but held its whole and solid firmness once for all, inseparably. Whoever tears and divides the Church of Christ cannot possess Christ's garment. Finally, when Solomon was dying and his kingdom and people were being divided, the prophet Ahijah met King Jeroboam in the field and tore his own garment into twelve pieces, saying: "Take ten pieces for yourself, for this is what the Lord says: 'Look, I am tearing the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and will give you ten scepters, and two scepters will remain his for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I chose to put my name there'" (1 Kings 11:30-32). When the twelve tribes of Israel were being divided, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But because the people of Christ cannot be divided, his tunic, woven throughout and holding together, was not divided by those who possessed it. Undivided, joined, connected, it shows the cohering harmony of our people who have put on Christ. By the sacred sign of the garment and its meaning, he declared the unity of the Church.

last_rejected.quote: to see who would rather put on Christ
last_rejected.why: "potius" means "rather" in sense of casting lots to determine who would put Christ on, not preference; "rather" misleads as preference.
last_rejected.fix: to see who would put on Christ
last_rejected.ruling: 'potius' with 'quis...indueret' naturally means 'who would rather put on Christ'; casting lots implies preference. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: which could not be torn at all by the one who received and possessed it
last_rejected.source_quote: quae ab accipiente ac possidente scindi omnino non poterat
last_rejected.why: Ablative singular "accipiente ac possidente" refers to Christ as the one receiving/possessing unity from above, not generic "one"; agency obscured.
last_rejected.fix: which could not be torn at all by him who received and possessed it
last_rejected.ruling: 'ab accipiente ac possidente' is ablative of agent/means; 'the one who received and possessed it' is correct. Christ is subject 'ille,' not the receiver.

last_rejected.quote: and two scepters will remain his
last_rejected.why: "erunt ei" means "will be to him/for him" (two tribes remain to Solomon), not "remain his" which suggests continued possession; slightly different claim.
last_rejected.fix: and two scepters will be his
last_rejected.ruling: 'erunt ei' = 'will be his/for him'; 'remain his' is within normal range. No meaning change; two tribes kept by Solomon.
